introduction-the-root-user-problem.core: Even with strong IAM, anyone with root on an EC2 instance (or malware running as root) can read process memory, keys and decrypted data. Nitro Enclaves create isolated compute environments on the instance with no persistent storage, no interactive access and no external networking, so highly sensitive processing is protected even from the instance's own administrators.

first_principles.problem: A payment service decrypts card data in memory on an instance that several admins can SSH into.
truths: Minimising the trusted computing base reduces risk.
derivation: Communicate only via **vsock** with the parent.

analogy.title: A sealed vault room inside a bank branch
analogy.story: Even the branch manager can't enter; documents go in and out through a slot.
analogy.breaks: Vault rooms have doors for emergencies; enclaves have no interactive access at all.

example.title: Card decryption
flow: Before: decrypt in app process on host

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Root on the host can't read card numbers.

check.q: What access does a Nitro Enclave allow the parent instance's root user?
check.a: None to its memory or processes; communication is only via the vsock channel.

architecture-the-isolated-sibling.core: An enclave is a separate VM carved out of the parent instance's vCPUs and memory by the Nitro Hypervisor. It runs a signed enclave image file (EIF) built from a Docker image, has its own kernel, no disk, no network interfaces and no console, and talks only to its parent over a local vsock socket.

first_principles.problem: Engineers expect an enclave to be a container and try to give it network access or volumes.
truths: Hypervisor isolation is stronger than containers.
derivation: Build an **EIF** with nitro-cli from a Docker image.
Proxy needed external calls through the **parent** (e.g. vsock-proxy to KMS).

analogy.title: A sibling living in a soundproof room next door
analogy.story: Same house, separate walls, and you talk only through a small hatch.
analogy.breaks: Siblings can leave the room; enclaves can't reach anything except via the parent.

steps.label: Output
steps.detail: Build prints PCR0/1/2 measurements used for attestation.

code.text:
nitro-cli build-enclave --docker-uri signer:latest --output-file signer.eif
nitro-cli run-enclave --eif-path signer.eif --cpu-count 2 --memory 2048 --enclave-cid 16

check.q: How does an enclave reach KMS if it has no network?
check.a: Through a proxy on the parent instance (e.g. vsock-proxy) forwarding traffic over vsock.

cryptographic-attestation-the-id-badge.core: The Nitro Hypervisor produces a signed attestation document containing the enclave's measurements (PCRs: hashes of the image, kernel, application and IAM role), plus a public key. KMS key policies can require specific PCR values (kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384), so only the exact, unmodified enclave can decrypt, and the response is encrypted to the enclave's key.

first_principles.problem: How does KMS know it's talking to the genuine enclave code and not a modified copy on the parent?
truths: Hardware-signed documents can't be forged by the host.
derivation: KMS returns data **encrypted to the enclave's public key**.

analogy.title: A tamper-proof ID badge issued by the building itself
analogy.story: Security checks the badge's hologram, not what the person claims.
analogy.breaks: Badges can be lost; attestation documents are generated fresh per request.

check.q: What does PCR0 represent in a Nitro Enclave attestation?
check.a: A hash of the enclave image file (EIF).

resource-allocation-stealing-from-the-pa.core: Enclaves take dedicated vCPUs (full cores) and memory away from the parent instance, configured in the allocator service (/etc/nitro_enclaves/allocator.yaml) before launch. The parent keeps the rest. Size enclaves for their workload, and choose instance types with enough cores (at least 4 vCPUs on most families) to leave capacity for the parent.

first_principles.problem: Launching an enclave fails, or the parent app slows dramatically after allocating resources.
truths: Cores are allocated in whole units.

analogy.title: Partitioning an office floor with a permanent wall
analogy.story: The secure room gets its desks; everyone else works in the remaining space.
analogy.breaks: Office walls are permanent; you can reallocate when no enclave runs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: On an 8-vCPU/32 GiB instance, parent keeps 6 vCPUs and 28 GiB.

check.q: Do enclaves share CPU with the parent instance?
check.a: No; they receive dedicated vCPUs (and memory) removed from the parent.
